newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel force is an eccentric mix.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel force is an eccentric mix.

text.p: Their uniforms vary, their languages differ and their roots are wide. But the disparate rebel force that has routed government troops and cleared refugee camps in eastern Zaire is united in purpose.
"Our target is to reach Kinshasha," says rebel leader Laurent Kabila. "Our next step is to launch an offensive which will take us further into eastern Zaire."
Whatever their goal, the rebel force is a sight to behold. Uniforms vary from the sublime -- regular camouflage -- to the faintly ridiculous -- bright red shirts, red jeans and wellington boots.
Even their transport has been turned into the bizarre.

Their vehicles, most stolen from aid agencies, are wildly painted -- some as zebras, some as tigers, some as giant, moving chequerboards, and one plastered with the handprints of the rebels who had commandeered it.
But the question many analysts are asking of the rebel force which has scored stunning victories in eastern Zaire is: to what extent is it backed by Rwanda?
Military commanders in Gisenyi and the Rwandan government have officially denied any involvement, but ground observation and anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise.
"We are made up from every ethnic grouping here (Zaire) and we have not received help from Rwanda or any other country," said Kabila.
Andre Kisasa, his military commander, agrees: "I have had no dealings or meetings with the Rwandan government and we have not received any help from any other country."
Officially the rebels are ethnic Zaireans who, in the course of battling government troops, also besieged refugee camps which have been home to over one million Rwandan Hutus since 1994.
Among the refugees were thousands of dreaded Interahamwe Hutus, responsible for the slaughter of up to one million Tutsis.

The Interahamwe have fled, pursued by the rebels, but ask any Zairean in the area who was responsible for putting their admittedly ill-disciplined army to flight and sparking the refugee exodus and you get one answer, Rwanda.

Whoever is in charge is at pains to ensure the Zairean element has a high profile. When Goma, the provincial capital of Kivu, was abandoned by government troops last week, Zairean rebels patrolled the streets.
But a Reuters correspondent came across a Rwandan officer he knew drinking at a hotel in the town -- clearly embarrassed to be discovered.
Reuters journalists also filmed the Rwandan army moving into Zaire during the fighting and saw them fighting Zairean troops in Goma.
Local drivers, interpreters and translators have had conversations with soldiers who admit they are Rwandans and frequently ask for messages to be passed to Kigali.
One soldier pretended first to be an Anglophone Zairean, then Ugandan before finally admitting to being a Rwandan.
English is clearly the common language for the rebels, although French, Kinyarwanda, Kiswahili and Kinande, a dialect of western Uganda, are also spoken.
Their weapons include 60mm mortar launchers, RPG7 rockets, every type of AK rifle, South African G4s and Israeli Uzis.
Their tactics -- similar to those of the Tutsi-led Rwandan army -- are a cross between the classic British "section and platoon attacks" and guerilla methods.

Whatever the mix, discipline among troops is good and relations with journalists cordial -- an attitude summed up by a T-shirt worn by one of the rebels which sported a picture of a skiing pig with the caption: "Don't bother me, I'm on the piste".
